The varieties of these actions Have been announced in many ways."},"philosophy":{"insight":"The Buddha taught two types of action: cetanā (intention/volition — the mental act) and cetayitvā (intentional — the physical/verbal acts arising from intention). Multiple classifications exist. The key: karma is rooted in INTENTION, not just outward behavior.","madhyamaka":"The Buddha (Unsurpassed Sage) distinguished cetanā (mental volition itself — the primary karma) from cetayitvā karmāṇi (actions done through intention — physical and verbal karma). Various classifications exist for pedagogical purposes. All are conventionally valid, ultimately empty.","quantum":"Measurement choice in QM: the experimenter's decision of what to measure (intention) shapes the experimental setup and determines which properties are observed (intentional action). The measurement choice is primary; the physical setup follows from it.","bridge":"Both Buddhist ethics and QM place primacy on the \"mental\" or \"choice\" element. Buddhism: intention is primary, physical/verbal actions follow. QM: measurement choice is primary, observed properties follow. Both: the \"mental\" element shapes the \"physical\" outcome.","accessible":"Your actions have two parts: (1) what you INTEND (your mental motivation) and (2) what you DO (your physical/verbal behavior). The Buddha said the intention is the more important part — the same external action with different intentions has different karmic results.","twoTruths":"Conventionally, intention and intentional actions are distinct and ethically significant. Ultimately, both are empty — dependently arisen mental and physical events without inherent essence.","commonMisconception":"NOT saying only intention matters (antinomianism). Both intention AND action matter conventionally. But intention is PRIMARY — the same act with different intentions produces different karmic results."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Measurement Choice Primacy","score":58,"strength":"Medium","explanation":"In QM, the choice of measurement determines what properties are observed. Intention determines ethical quality.","realLifeExample":"Accidentally stepping on an insect vs. deliberately crushing one. Same physical result; vastly different moral weight. Intention makes the difference."},{"q":"What are the \"varieties\" of action?","a":"Multiple classification systems: by ethical quality (virtuous/nonvirtuous/neutral), by mode (body/speech/mind), by realm (desire/form/formless), by result (merit/demerit/neither). Each classification serves a pedagogical purpose.","realLifeExample":"Scientists classify animals by different systems (species, habitat, diet). Each classification highlights different features. Similarly, Buddhist action-classifications highlight different ethical aspects."},{"q":"How does emptiness apply to intention?","a":"Intention itself is dependently arisen — arising from conditions (past habits, current stimuli, mental factors). It lacks inherent essence. An \"inherent intention\" would be permanent and unchangeable — you could never change your mind or develop new motivations.","realLifeExample":"If your intention were inherent, you could never change your values or grow ethically. The fact that people change their minds and develop morally proves intentions lack inherent essence."},{"q":"Does QM measurement choice truly parallel intention?","a":"Loosely: in QM, what you choose to measure determines what you can observe. Choosing compassion vs. anger determines the quality of your action.
